summary: Static electricity for ages 11–12: rubbing two insulators together does not create charge, it transfers electrons from one material to the other, leaving one negative (gained electrons) and the other equally positive (lost electrons). Like charges repel and unlike attract, with the force acting across a gap and strengthening with more charge and smaller separation. A charged object also attracts a neutral one by inducing/polarising its charge, so only repulsion proves two like charges. A discharge is electrons jumping along a newly available path — a spark or, at huge scale, lightning. A dynamic model that makes the invisible electron transfer visible, countable and conserved may be combined with direct testing of the force rule on suspended charged objects, kept qualitative to match assessment limits; the sources do not establish that this combination outperforms other media.
misconceptions: 'Rubbing creates charge / makes electricity' — charge is conserved; rubbing only TRANSFERS electrons from one object to the other.
'Protons / positive charges move' — in solids only electrons move; the positively charged object did not gain positives, it LOST electrons.
Thinking both rubbed objects get the same sign of charge — they get OPPOSITE charges (one gains the electrons the other loses).
Believing attraction proves the other object is oppositely charged — a charged object also attracts a NEUTRAL one by induction/polarisation; only REPULSION proves two like charges.
Confusing static charge with current — static is charge held still with no flow path (often on insulators); current is charge flowing in a complete circuit.
Thinking charged objects must touch to exert a force — the force acts across a gap (the electric-field idea), strengthening with more charge and smaller separation.
Believing lightning only travels cloud-to-ground — discharge can occur within a cloud, cloud-to-cloud, or ground-to-cloud; it is charge separation neutralising along any available path.
Treating metals as where static builds up — charge accumulates on INSULATORS; on a conductor it would flow away to earth.

activities.title: Counting electrons: rubbing moves charge, it does not make it
steps: Start from two neutral objects shown with equal numbers of positive and negative charges (e.g. a balloon and a head of hair, or a polythene rod and a cloth).
Rub them together and watch individual electrons hop one by one from one material onto the other, with a running tally of each object's charge.
Read the tally after rubbing: confirm the balloon/rod is negative by exactly the number of electrons the hair/cloth lost, which is now equally positive.
State in your own words where the charge came from: nothing was created; electrons were only moved, so the two objects carry equal and opposite charge.
activities.insight: Charge is conserved: rubbing separates and transfers existing electrons rather than generating new charge, and in solids it is the negative electrons that move, so the positive object is positive precisely because it lost them.

activities.title: Attract or repel? Testing the force rule across a gap
steps: Predict, before releasing, whether two objects rubbed the same way (e.g. two balloons rubbed on wool, or two like-charged rods) will swing together or apart, and give a reason.
Suspend the two charged objects on threads and bring them close; observe that they repel and swing apart.
Bring a charged balloon near a NEUTRAL wall and watch it lean in and stick as the wall's charges shuffle (induction/polarisation).
Compare the two outcomes and decide: what does repulsion tell you about the two charges, and why does attraction NOT prove the other object is oppositely charged?
Vary the amount of charge and the separation (e.g. with sliders or by moving objects nearer) and describe qualitatively how the force changes.
activities.insight: Like charges repel and unlike attract, but attraction alone is ambiguous because a charged object also attracts a neutral one by induction; only repulsion confirms two like charges. The force acts across a gap and strengthens with more charge and smaller distance.

activities.title: From spark to lightning: discharge as charge flowing back
steps: With built-up charge on an object, give the electrons a path (e.g. press a 'discharge' control, or touch a metal handle after rubbing) and observe the spark.
Describe what the spark is: the separated electrons flowing to neutralise the charge difference once a path exists.
Zoom out to a thundercloud and relate cloud charge separation and a lightning strike to the same discharge process at a far larger scale.
Explain how static (charge held still, often on an insulator, with no flow path) and current (charge flowing in a complete circuit) are related — a discharge is a brief flow of the same charge.
Consider that lightning can travel within a cloud, cloud-to-cloud, or ground-to-cloud, not only cloud-to-ground.
activities.insight: A discharge is separated charge neutralising along any available path; static (charge at rest) and current (charge in motion) are two states of the same charge, and lightning is a city-scale version of a doorknob spark.

activities.title: Check your reasoning: signs, forces and discharge
steps: Given two named materials rubbed together, choose which way electrons move and the resulting sign of each object.
Sort pairs of charged objects into those that attract and those that repel.
Answer whether attraction proves the other object is oppositely charged, and explain (no — it could be neutral and attracted by induction).
Complete: 'Rubbing transfers ____; it does not create charge.'
Explain in a sentence or two how a doorknob spark and lightning are the same process.
activities.insight: Consolidate the mechanism and rules: direction of electron transfer, resulting opposite charges, like/unlike forces, the ambiguity of attraction, and discharge as flowing charge.

checkQuestion: You rub a plastic rod with a cloth and the rod becomes negatively charged. What happens to the cloth — is it charged now, and if so how is it charged? Explain where the rod's extra charge came from.
checkAnswer: The cloth becomes positively charged. Rubbing did not make any new charge — it transferred electrons from the cloth onto the rod. The rod gained electrons (negative), so the cloth is left with an equal and opposite positive charge. Charge is separated and moved, not created.
